extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, life-sciences inventors, and IP professionals interested in §101 eligibility for diagnostic claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-law-based criteria for evaluating whether diagnostic method claims in the life sciences are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 following Mayo, Myriad, and Alice. Focuses on how courts and the USPTO apply the two-step Mayo/Alice test to diagnostic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-step test for patent eligibility: (1) determine whether claims are directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea); (2) if so, determine whether claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claimed exception into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is not directed to an exception under step 1, it is patent-eligible. If step 1 is met (claim directed to an exception), courts proceed to step 2 to search for an inventive concept. The article repeatedly applies this framework to diagnostic method claims and ties each case outcome to the two-step analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-to-exception inquiry (Step 1): law of nature / natural phenomenon / abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 asks whether the claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept such as a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found claims 'directed to' natural laws/phenomena when they claim correlations or relationships discovered by the inventors (examples: relationships between metabolite concentrations and drug efficacy in Mayo; existence of cffDNA in maternal plasma in Ariosa; linkage between non-coding and coding sequences in Genetic Techs.; MPO level correlation with cardiovascular risk in Cleveland Clinic). If the core of the claim is that discovered correlation/phenomenon, step 1 is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement (Step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: After step 1 finds a claim directed to an exception, step 2 requires looking for an 'inventive concept'—additional elements that transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept must do more than simply state the ineligible concept plus conventional steps. The courts evaluate whether the additional elements meaningfully limit or transform the claim beyond the natural law or phenomenon itself. Examples throughout the article show claims failing step 2 when only routine techniques or generic steps were appended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity does not supply an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps or techniques that are well-known, conventional, or routine at the time of filing generally cannot supply the inventive concept required by step 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly characterized techniques such as preparing samples, amplifying DNA (PCR), sequencing, using probes, detection techniques, iodination, and immunoprecipitation as 'well-understood, routine and conventional' and thus insufficient to transform a natural phenomenon into a patentable claim (see Myriad, Ariosa, Genetic Techs., Cleveland Clinic, Athena). Even applying known techniques to a newly discovered natural phenomenon may be held insufficient (Ariosa, Genetic Techs.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely recite a discovery of a correlation + routine steps will likely be ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that consist essentially of (a) identifying a natural correlation or phenomenon and (b) appending conventional laboratory or detection steps to observe that correlation typically fail the Mayo/Alice test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple Federal Circuit decisions invalidated diagnostic method claims on this basis: Mayo (metabolite correlations), Ariosa (cffDNA detection steps appended to natural phenomenon), Genetic Techs. (linkage correlation plus amplification/analysis), Cleveland Clinic (MPO correlation + normal detection). The article emphasizes that such claims 'merely tell those interested in the subject about the correlations that the researchers discovered.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth matters — narrowly tailored claims may fare better than broad claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly drafted diagnostic claims that encompass the natural correlation plus generic steps have fared poorly; it remains possible that narrow, specifically tailored diagnostic claims could survive the Mayo/Alice test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that most claims invalidated post-Mayo were broad and that whether a narrowly-tailored claim could pass step 2 is an open question. This indicates claim scope is an important factor in eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble/claim language and added diagnosis steps can change eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Small differences in claim wording (e.g., reciting 'detecting JUL-1' vs. 'diagnosing julitis') can alter whether a claim is considered directed to a natural law and thus whether it survives step 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO Example 29 is highlighted: Claim 1 (detecting JUL-1) was treated as patent-eligible under Step 1, whereas Claim 2, which added an explicit 'diagnosing' limitation, was treated as directed to the natural law (correlation between JUL-1 and disease) and held ineligible. The example drew public criticism for seeming arbitrary; claim drafter should be mindful how preamble and added outcome/diagnosis language can affect the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of man-made molecules or reagents does not automatically confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting a man-made molecule or reagent in a claim does not necessarily make a claim patent-eligible if the claim is directed to detecting or exploiting a natural phenomenon rather than to creating or inventing the man-made molecule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Athena, the court found that including a radiolabeled MuSK (a man-made molecule) did not make the diagnostic claims eligible because the claims were directed to detecting autoantibodies (a natural phenomenon) rather than creating the radiolabeled molecule. The lesson: claiming the production/creation of a non-natural thing is different from claiming its use in detection; only the former is more likely to contribute to eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claims may be treated differently when they involve human-made alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to compositions that are not naturally occurring (e.g., cDNA lacking introns) can be patent-eligible because they are not naturally occurring, whereas mere isolation of natural products may not be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad held that isolated genomic DNA was not patent-eligible because the nucleotide sequence existed in nature, but cDNA (exon-only sequence) was eligible because it does not occur in nature. Thus composition claims that involve human-made structural changes can avoid the natural-product exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim assessment can be done limitation-by-limitation or considering the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may analyze claims element-by-element and/or consider the claim as a whole when determining whether additional elements provide an inventive concept under step 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleveland Clinic is cited for the court's approach in which it examined claims both limitation-by-limitation and as an entirety and concluded the claims did not 'sufficiently transform' the natural correlation. Drafters should consider both perspectives when evaluating claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual inquiry into whether techniques were standard may be required (possible discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claimed steps were 'standard' or 'conventional' at the time of filing can be a factual question requiring discovery and further factual development in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Athena the district court initially indicated discovery was needed to determine whether techniques were standard; after discovery the court found the techniques to be standard and invalidated the claims. This shows that the eligibility outcome can depend on factual record about what was routine in the art at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative guidance and case law can yield inconsistent or unpredictable outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO guidance (e.g., Example 29) and court decisions have sometimes reached different or seemingly inconsistent conclusions for similar claim language, producing uncertainty in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes public criticism of USPTO Example 29 for treating two nearly identical claims differently and observes that courts and the USPTO have struggled to apply the Mayo/Alice framework consistently. Practitioners should be aware of this unpredictability and the potential for differing outcomes across tribunals and claim drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent bindingness and judicially perceived constraints affect outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some judges have expressed that they disagree with certain eligibility outcomes but feel constrained to follow Supreme Court precedent (Mayo), which can produce outcomes contrary to some judges' views of what should be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Ariosa some judges stated they thought the claims should be patent-eligible but felt bound by Mayo. This underscores the importance of both legal argument and the current state of precedent when evaluating eligibility prospects.
